fable-5.1.text:
So, one way I like to think about it is that human learning doesn't look like any of the things we do, at least not cleanly. It's not pre-training, and it's not RL in the way we do RL. It has pieces of both, but the proportions are completely different.

Here's what I mean. If you look at a human, there's clearly something like a prior, which evolution gave us. Evolution did a huge amount of, let's say, compute, over a very long time, and the result is a brain that is already set up to learn certain things very easily. Language, vision, social stuff, physical intuition. So you could say evolution is the pre-training, and the lifetime of the person is the fine-tuning. But if you say it that way, you immediately notice that the "fine-tuning" is doing an enormous amount. A person learns a huge number of things in their lifetime that evolution could not possibly have anticipated. And they learn them from a very small amount of data.

And that's really the striking thing. The sample efficiency. A teenager learns to drive in, I don't know, ten hours. Ten hours of actual practice, and then they're pretty competent. They're not perfect, but they're competent, and they generalize. They drive on a road they've never seen. Compare that to what we do, where you need millions of episodes, and even then the generalization is kind of fragile. So whatever humans are doing, the generalization is much more robust and it comes from much less experience.

The other thing I'd point to is that humans seem to have something like a value function, and a very good one. When you're working on a problem, you don't need to get to the end and then be told "correct" or "incorrect." You have a sense, partway through, that this is going well or this is not going well. You feel it. And I actually think emotions are a big part of this. Emotions are, in some sense, a value function that evolution hard-coded, and then you refine it over your life. And it's very robust. It doesn't fall apart when you're in a situation you haven't seen before. That's a big difference from what we do now, where the reward is very narrow and comes only at the end, and the model has to be in exactly the right kind of environment for it to work at all.

And then there is the continual aspect. A person is just always learning. There's no separate training phase and deployment phase. You go through your day, you do things, you make mistakes, and then you're a little bit different the next day. And it's not that you memorized the episode. You extracted something from it. You updated in a way that's very targeted and very compact.

So if you forced me to put it in ML language, I would say: a strong evolutionary prior, a very good and very general value function, continual learning from an extremely small amount of data, and generalization that is far better than anything we currently know how to get. And I think the honest thing to say is that we don't really understand why the generalization is so good. We have hints. But the thing that makes a human learn to drive in ten hours, we don't have that. And I think figuring out what that is, is really what the next few years are going to be about.

opus-5.5.text:
I think the most striking thing about human learning, in machine-learning terms, is how sample-efficient and robust it is. A teenager learns to drive in something like ten hours of practice, and they're pretty good at it. They don't need millions of examples. And they're not just memorizing; they generalize to new roads, new weather, new situations they've never seen. Our models, by comparison, need enormous amounts of data, and even then the generalization can be strangely brittle. They'll do something brilliant on an eval and then make a basic mistake that no person would make.

You might say evolution gave us a really good prior, and that's part of it. For vision, for locomotion, for things our ancestors did for hundreds of millions of years, I believe that. But people learn math, programming, and other things that evolution couldn't possibly have prepared us for, and they learn them quickly. So it's not only a prior. There seems to be something about the learning algorithm itself that's just better.

The other piece I find really interesting is something like a value function. When a person is learning, they don't wait until the very end of a long task to find out whether they did well. They have an internal sense, as they go, of "this is going well" or "this isn't working." Emotions probably play a big role here. They're a fairly simple, robust signal that evolution hardcoded, and they let you learn continuously from your own experience without anyone grading you. People also learn continually: you're deployed in the world and learning at the same time, not trained once and then frozen.

So in ML terms I'd say human learning is continual, extremely sample-efficient, generalizes far better, and is guided by a strong built-in value function. Figuring out what underlies that is, I think, one of the most important questions right now.

fable-5.text:
So the interesting thing about human learning is that it doesn't map cleanly onto either of the two paradigms we have in machine learning. It's not pretraining, and it's not reinforcement learning as we practice it, though it has some flavor of both.

Consider a teenager learning to drive. After maybe ten hours of practice, they become a pretty reliable driver. Ten hours. There is no pretraining corpus of driving. There's no huge number of rollouts with a reward at the end. And yet the learning is extremely sample efficient and, importantly, extremely robust. The teenager doesn't just learn to drive — they know what they don't know. They feel uncertain in the right situations. They self-correct in real time without anyone giving them a reward signal.

So in machine-learning terms, I would say humans have several things we don't yet know how to build. One is that they seem to have a very good value function. You don't need to finish the drive and crash the car to get a learning signal — you feel, moment to moment, "this is going well" or "this is getting dangerous," and you learn from that immediately. Our emotions are, in some sense, a value function that evolution has given us, and it's a surprisingly robust and useful one.

The second thing is that the human prior is not like pretraining. People sometimes say, well, evolution is the human's pretraining. But the amount of information evolution can pass through the genome is tiny compared to what our models consume. It's much more like evolution found an incredibly good learning algorithm and a small amount of very well-chosen structure, and then the person does the rest from a modest amount of experience. Whereas with our models, we compensate for a weaker learning algorithm with astronomically more data.

And the third thing, which I think is underrated, is the robustness. Human learning generalizes in this very smooth way. When a person is good at something, they're good at it in a rounded, reliable way — the skill doesn't have these strange jagged edges where it works on the benchmark and falls apart just outside it. That difference in generalization, more than raw capability, is to me the clearest signature that humans are doing something our methods don't yet capture.

opus-5.text:
I think the most striking thing — and it's so familiar that people stop noticing it — is how little data a human needs. A fifteen-year-old learns to drive in maybe ten hours of practice, and that's with no prior driving experience of any kind. Self-driving cars have orders and orders of magnitude more than that, and arguably they're still not quite there. So whatever humans are doing, it's a dramatically more sample-efficient learning algorithm than what we have.

Now the obvious objection is: well, evolution did a huge amount of pretraining, right? Millions of years. And I think that objection is weaker than it sounds. The amount of information in the genome is actually quite small, and whatever is in there, it's not *knowledge* in the sense that a pretrained model has knowledge. It's more like a very good architecture and a very good learning algorithm and maybe a very good value function. The lion cub that walks shortly after birth — that's not a lot of bits. But the human teenager learning to drive, that's not drawing on inherited driving facts. It's drawing on a learning procedure.

The other thing I'd point to is that humans are doing something that's much more like continual learning than like our train-then-deploy setup. A person who starts a new job is bad at it for three months and then good at it, and the thing that changed is not that they read more of the internet. They had experience, they made mistakes, they had a feeling about what went wrong, and they updated. And crucially they updated in a way that didn't destroy everything else they knew.

And then there's the emotional piece, which I think is underrated and genuinely closer to a technical claim than it sounds. Emotions look a lot like a value function — a compact, fast, evolutionarily-tuned signal about whether things are going well, which can guide learning over long horizons where the actual reward is very sparse. Our models have something much cruder there.

So if I had to compress it: humans are not pretrained in the way our models are. They're a very good learning algorithm with a decent value function, running online, forever, on a tiny data stream. That combination is the thing I think we don't have yet.

sonnet-5.5.text:
One thing that stands out to me is how little data people need. A teenager can learn to drive in about ten hours, and they get there without anything like the enormous pile of examples we give our models. What they learn is also robust. They don't just pattern-match to the situations they were taught in. They carry it over to new ones.

So if I put it in machine-learning terms, I'd say human learning is, first, extremely sample-efficient. Second, it generalizes much better than what we have today. Third, it doesn't need a clean, hand-specified reward. A person can learn in an unsupervised-ish way, with no one handing them a verifiable signal at every step. Their own internal sense of whether things are going well or badly guides them, and they can correct themselves along the way. It's hard to say precisely what that is, but I think it's a big part of why learning looks so different in people.

Some of it is probably prior knowledge from evolution. For vision, hearing, and locomotion, it's plausible that evolution gave us a lot, and that would explain why we're so good at those. But language, math, and programming are very recent, and people still pick them up quickly. That suggests there's something more fundamental going on than a good built-in prior, some better machinery for learning itself.

The gap I keep coming back to is this: our models can look superhuman on benchmarks and then fail in ways that feel strangely brittle. A person who is good at something usually understands it more robustly. I think that gap is the heart of the problem, and until we understand it better, I'm not sure just scaling what we have will close it.

haiku-5.5.text:
I'd start with the fact that still bothers me most. A person learns to drive in a few dozen hours, and a child learns what a dog is from a handful of examples. Our models need orders of magnitude more data to reach anything comparable. So whatever the brain is doing, it has a much better learning algorithm, or much better priors, or both.

I think a big part of it is that evolution has already done a lot of the work. Humans arrive with strong inductive biases, shaped over an enormous amount of time, and those biases make the learning that happens within a lifetime far more efficient. Then there's ongoing experience. We aren't trained once on a fixed dataset. We act, we see what happens, and we update continuously, with feedback that is rich and often immediate.

I also think we underrate the role of internal signals. Emotions and intuitions behave something like value functions. They tell you early whether a path is promising, long before the final outcome arrives. That kind of signal is very useful for learning efficiently.

So if I had to put it in machine-learning terms, I'd say human learning looks like sample-efficient, self-directed learning with strong priors, a continuous stream of experience, and dense internal feedback. Getting machines to do something similar is, I think, one of the central open problems.

astra-6.text:
Well, I don’t think human learning fits neatly into one category. There’s something like self-supervised learning: you observe the world, and you learn how it works without someone telling you the right answer at every moment. There’s reinforcement learning: you try things, you see what happens, and you change your behavior. And of course, people can explain things to you.

But the really interesting question is: what are you starting with? A human is not a randomly initialized neural network. Evolution has done a tremendous amount of work to produce a brain that can learn. So when we say a person learned something from two examples, those two examples are interacting with a very rich starting point, plus everything that person has already experienced.

I think the hard part is understanding how much of that efficiency comes from the starting point, and how much comes from the learning process itself.

sol-6.1.text:
I think we don’t have a completely satisfactory answer. You can recognize elements of self-supervised learning: you observe the world, you form expectations, and you update when something surprising happens. And there’s reinforcement learning: you try things, some outcomes are good, some are bad, and that changes your behavior.

But the starting point matters enormously. A human isn’t a randomly initialized neural network. Evolution has already done a huge amount of work to produce a brain that learns particular things very efficiently. In machine-learning terms, there’s an outer optimization process that produces the system that then does the learning.

The interesting question is what exactly evolution has supplied. Is it mostly the architecture? Is it the learning algorithm? Is it certain objectives or predispositions? Probably some combination. Saying that humans do self-supervised learning and reinforcement learning captures something, but it doesn’t yet explain why we can learn so much from so little experience.

So when a person learns a new concept from one or two examples, they’re fitting it into a structure they already have. In machine-learning terms, it’s a combination of extensive pretraining, active learning, and continual adaptation.

terra-5.6.text: I think it’s a mixture. There’s a tremendous amount of self-supervised learning: you’re constantly observing the world and implicitly learning to predict what will happen next. There’s also reinforcement learning—rewards, punishments, social approval, emotions—but I don’t think that’s the whole story. And, crucially, humans come with an enormous prior from evolution, which makes us extraordinarily sample-efficient compared with a system that starts from scratch.

sol-5.6.text: I think human learning is often misunderstood. A child may seem to learn from very little data, but by the time they learn a particular task, they already have an enormous amount of prior experience—and their brain is the product of evolution. In machine-learning terms, evolution supplies a very strong architecture and prior, childhood supplies a vast amount of self-supervised pretraining, and what we ordinarily call “learning” is often just fine-tuning on top of that. So humans are not really learning from scratch from a few examples; they are bringing a huge amount of structure and accumulated experience to those examples.

luna-5.6.text: Human learning is remarkably efficient because it’s largely self-supervised. We learn by predicting what happens next, building an internal model of the world, and then using relatively small amounts of labeled feedback to refine it. But humans also have strong inductive biases, embodied experience, and the ability to reason and act in the world. So in machine-learning terms, I’d say we’re doing multimodal self-supervised learning, followed by continual reinforcement learning, with a very powerful prior about how the world works.
